cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\), there exists an integer \(q\ge2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish the following two classes of explicitly listed Unique Games instances over the alphabet \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\):
\[\text{YES: }\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad \text{NO: }\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta.\]
NP-hardness here means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT with the completeness and soundness guarantees defined below. The alphabet size and the reduction may depend on the two constants but must be fixed before the input size grows. The target is this hardness proposition itself, without assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
cards.definitions:
Instance and value. An instance has a finite vertex set \(V=[n]\) with \(n\ge2\), an ordered nonempty list of \(m\ge1\) directed edges \((u_j,v_j)\) with distinct endpoints in \(V\), and a permutation \(\pi_j:[q]\to[q]\) for each edge index \(j\in[m]\). Repeated directed edges, including repeated constraints or different constraints on the same ordered pair, are allowed and counted separately. There is no restriction on degree, expansion, connectedness or bipartiteness, and isolated vertices are allowed. A permutation is a bijection: each label occurs exactly once among its \(q\) images. A labeling is one map \(\ell:V\to[q]\), with no probabilistic or quantum strategy. Edge \(j\) is satisfied when \(\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\). Define
\[\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_{\ell:V\to[q]}\frac{|\{j\in[m]:\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\}|}{m}.\]
The finite maximum is attained and lies in \([0,1]\). All edge occurrences have equal weight. Reversing an edge would require using the inverse permutation; its stored direction fixes the equation used here. The two promised classes are disjoint because \(\delta<1-\varepsilon\). Instances with \(\delta<\operatorname{val}(G)<1-\varepsilon\) are outside the promise.

Explicit encoding. Vertex labels and all integers are written in binary with length prefixes. Concretely, a nonnegative integer \(z\) may be encoded by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). A game encoding lists \(q,n,m\), all \(n\) vertex labels in order, and for each edge its two endpoints followed by the entire table \(\pi_j(1),\ldots,\pi_j(q)\). Tables are not circuits or oracles representing longer objects. Input and output lengths count every listed bit. This convention fixes a finite-string model; polynomially interconvertible standard explicit encodings give the same hardness question.

Reduction and source problem. A 3CNF formula \(\varphi\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each an ordered disjunction of three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable \(x_i\) or its negation. Repeated literals are allowed. List the variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_s\) and the clauses, recording literal signs as bits and indices and list lengths with the integer encoding above. The empty conjunction is allowed and is true. A satisfying assignment is a map from these variables to \(\{0,1\}\) making every clause true. Let \(|\varphi|\) be the full bit length of this encoding. For fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta,q\), the required reduction is a single deterministic Turing-machine program \(F\) for which some constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) bound its time by \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\) on every valid formula. Time includes writing the output. On each such formula it must output one valid game \(G=F(\varphi)\) over exactly \([q]\), satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\le\delta.\]
Thus both kinds of formulas map into the promise. A multi-tape deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes suffices as the computation model; each transition reads and writes one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. No advice, randomness or oracle is allowed. Behavior on malformed formula strings is immaterial. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is the meaning of NP-hardness used here; no decision algorithm for the game is part of the requested reduction.

Parameter quantifiers. The order is \(\forall(\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists q\ \exists F,C,k\ \forall\varphi\). The machine, alphabet, time exponent and constant may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but not on the formula. The parameters are not growing input variables, and no common polynomial exponent or effective procedure selecting reductions for all parameters is additionally required. Restricting the gap parameters to positive rationals loses none of the usual real-parameter conjecture: smaller rational errors give the required inclusions of the real-parameter YES and NO classes. The usual one-error formulation is equivalent by taking the smaller of the two errors.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the entire quantified hardness proposition, including the deterministic reductions, polynomial output/time bounds, valid permutation constraints, and both implications for every formula, or prove its logical negation. A negative answer must identify fixed rational \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\) such that no alphabet \(q\ge2\) admits the required reduction. Equivalently, for each \(q\) and every deterministic polynomial-time candidate program, some valid 3CNF formula has an invalid output or violates its applicable YES/NO guarantee. This is a statement about all reductions, not just a failed construction or a particular alphabet. No unproved complexity assumption may replace the requested conclusion. A polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm alone does not logically refute the NP-hardness proposition without an appropriate separation such as \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Hardness with completeness bounded away from one, perfect satisfiability testing, a restricted graph class, or a result for many-to-one constraints does not by itself settle this target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

importance.reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute \(\alpha >0\), an \(\exp (q n^{\varepsilon ^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm finding a \((1- \varepsilon ^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling in a \((1- \varepsilon )\)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-\(\varepsilon\) regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness \(1/2\) and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.
Yoshida reports a sublinear-query tolerant tester with the additional condition \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\); this is not the unrestricted fixed-gap UGC regime.

Fei–Minzer–Wang claim perfect-completeness hardness for 4-to-1 games and consequent coloring hardness. Their introduction still separates full UGC as a conjecture; no independent certification of the new proof is asserted here.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The 14 September Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint explicitly retains UGC as Conjecture 1.4 while claiming perfect-completeness 4-to-1 hardness in Theorem 1.6; that theorem has different constraints and does not settle this card. The May tolerant tester has a size-dependent error restriction and does not cover the full fixed-gap target. No matching proof or refutation of UGC was found in the bounded primary-source search. The formulation is complete; the recent preprint proof and historical proof sequences were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally reversible: either endpoint label fixes exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Despite this simplicity, the conjecture asks whether an almost perfectly consistent collection is NP-hard to distinguish from one for which every labeling violates almost all constraints. This is a promise decision gap, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum.

For example, with two labels an identity permutation asks for equal labels, while a transposition asks for different labels. Three transposition constraints on the edges of a triangle have value \(2/3\). This illustrates how individually consistent requirements can conflict globally; the conjecture quantifies over larger alphabets and much more extreme gaps.

Exact satisfiability, meaning \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\), is polynomial-time decidable in this explicit model. The positive completeness error \(\varepsilon\) is therefore an essential feature of the conjecture. A uniformly random labeling satisfies an expected fraction \(1/q\) of the edges, so every instance has value at least \(1/q\). In particular, if \(\delta<1/q\), there are no NO instances. The alphabet cannot be fixed in advance of all soundness thresholds.

Raghavendra’s 2008 theorem ties Unique-Games-based hardness to a general semidefinite-programming framework for constraint satisfaction over a fixed finite domain. Under UGC, its approximation guarantees are optimal up to arbitrary fixed accuracy, with the usual consequence for polynomial-time algorithms requiring a complexity separation. This explains why one apparently narrow family of permutation constraints governs many approximation thresholds.

Arora, Barak and Steurer’s 2010 theorem gives, for an absolute \(\alpha>0\), an \(\exp(qn^{\varepsilon^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm returning a \((1-\varepsilon^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling on an \(n\)-vertex, \((1-\varepsilon)\)-satisfiable instance. For fixed \(q\) and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\), this is subexponential but does not give polynomial time. Its dependence on completeness is compatible with reductions whose polynomial exponent depends on the desired gap.

The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies that, for every fixed positive soundness threshold, Unique Games is NP-hard with completeness \(1/2\). Khot’s exposition states this as Theorem 2.20. The conclusion leaves the near-one completeness in UGC unresolved. The 2025 journal publication of one part of the proof sequence records the historical role of its conditional intermediate theorem and still states full UGC separately as Conjecture 1.4.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims the \(4\)-to-\(1\) Games Conjecture with perfect completeness. Its constraints are projections in which each right-hand label has four preimages, rather than bijections. Theorem 1.6 is a major related hardness claim, with graph-coloring consequences, but does not prove the permutation-constraint UGC. The same introduction retains UGC as Conjecture 1.4 and identifies completeness \(1/2\) as the existing Unique Games hardness frontier. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Yoshida’s May 2026 tolerant-testing preprint concerns adjacency-list queries and distinguishes small from larger optimum violation fractions. Its Theorem 1.1 requires \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\), where \(\rho\) is the larger violation threshold and \(c_q>0\) depends on the fixed alphabet. For the UGC gap, \(\rho=1-\delta\); the displayed assumption does not hold for every input size when the positive errors and alphabet are fixed. Thus the tester’s sublinear query bound does not refute this fixed-parameter, all-instance hardness statement.

sentences: A Unique Games instance consists of explicitly listed vertices and permutation constraints between pairs of labels.
UGC asks for NP-hardness of distinguishing almost completely satisfiable instances from those with arbitrarily small optimum value.
The alphabet and deterministic reduction may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but must be independent of the growing input formula.
A complete Lean proof must establish the full reduction statement or its negation over every alphabet and polynomial-time candidate reduction.
The September 2026 perfect-completeness 4-to-1 claim and the known half-completeness Unique Games theorem do not establish this near-one-completeness permutation-constraint conjecture.

No P-versus-NP assumption or common reduction exponent is silently inserted.

checked_sources: Read Khot 2010 survey full §2.4, Definition 2.4 and Conjecture 2.5, printed pp.5–6. The source uses arbitrary directed constraint graphs, uniform edge fractions, gap-dependent constant alphabet, and explicitly distinguishes perfect consistency and NP-hardness from the absence of algorithms. The card fixes exact finite encodings and does not reuse the survey’s informal P-not-NP assumptions as axioms.

Read Raghavendra STOC 2008 primary paper abstract, introduction, §1.1, Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Corollary 1.3. The algorithm/hardness correspondence is for a fixed finite-domain CSP and arbitrary constant accuracy. No claim that this proves UGC was made.

Read Arora–Barak–Steurer author manuscript dated 8 April 2010 abstract, full introductory theorem discussion, Theorem 1.1 and parameter footnote. The exp(q n^(epsilon^alpha)) bound depends on a fixed completeness error and alphabet, and the discussion expressly distinguishes it from an exp(n^o(1)) result for fixed error. It does not rule out parameter-dependent polynomial-size NP-hardness reductions.

Read Khot 2-to-2 exposition §2.8 Definition 2.18, Theorems 2.19–2.20, the exact-half-completeness padding discussion, and §2.9 opening consequences. The published claim is hardness at completeness exactly 1/2, not arbitrarily close to one.

Read official Theory of Computing 21(11) metadata and the published 50-page PDF abstract and §1.1 through the proof-sequence discussion. Published 26 November 2025, revised March 2024, preliminary STOC 2018. Definition 1.2 distinguishes d-to-1 from 1-to-1 and Conjecture 1.4 retains UGC. Corrected reference title to include the question mark printed on the PDF.

Read Fei–Minzer–Wang ECCC TR26-179 official record dated 14 September 2026 and full PDF abstract, §§1.1–1.2 and coloring consequences. Definition 1.3 distinguishes d-to-1; Conjecture 1.4 retains UGC; Theorem 1.6 asserts perfect-completeness 4-to-1 hardness. Used the theorem’s consistently quantified epsilon rather than the abstract’s epsilon/delta mismatch. The introduction explicitly retains half-completeness as the current UGC hardness frontier. The 95-page proof was not independently audited; author presentation caveat recorded. Existing active cards TCS-5544,7237,6637,3984 already reflect the new claim and were not overwritten.

Read Yoshida arXiv:2605.17760v1 official record and PDF §1 through Theorem 1.1 and model conventions. The assumption is epsilon log n <= c_Q rho^4 and the complexity is expected adjacency-list queries, success at least 2/3. Translating violation fraction to 1-value demonstrates why it does not cover every instance size for the fixed UGC parameters.

Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching proof or refutation. Screened arXiv:2609.05122 through its official abstract: noisy-entanglement repetition bounds concern a different game value and communication model. The 2026 robust PCSP and welfare results surfaced as conditional uses of UGC, not proofs. No exhaustive search or independent certification of external proofs is claimed; no archive card body was opened.

Checked exact logical negation, no uniform parameter selector, full explicit output cost, repeated literal/edge conventions, rational gap equivalence, and distinction between P-not-NP consequences and the literal hardness statement. Repaired malformed dollar delimiters and the original value formula.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
